description:
My name is CELY CELIA CONDOR ORIZANO. I am an attorney and an MBA student at CONTINENTAL UNIVERSITY FLORIDA. I am interested in technological innovation. My project focuses on climate change, and I propose developing a satellite application to analyze patterns and identify key locations where fires are likely to occur.

I invite participants to join us.
summary: Smart Forest Guardians turns NASA FIRMS satellite data into wildfire information anyone in Peru can understand and act on. For the challenge, we built a harmonized MODIS–VIIRS burning calendar from 25 years of FIRMS archives (2.4 million hotspots): users pick any area (department, province, drawn polygon or radius) and dates, see monthly activity and anomalies versus a normal year, and download CSV and PNG. VIIRS sees about 4 times more fires than MODIS, so we calibrate it to MODIS-equivalent and validate it leaving one year out. Our web map shows near-real-time fires with strength (FRP), wind, temperature, humidity, air quality, spread forecast and nearby towns; "My zone" gives a 50 or 100 km risk level, which authority to call (firefighters, police or SERFOR) and a WhatsApp report the user approves, and an AI assistant answers in simple Spanish using only real data. The web matters for planning: municipalities and SERFOR can see when and where fires repeat and prepare before the burning season. Our Android app (Kotlin) checks our alerts API every 15 minutes and notifies citizens (20 km) and firefighters (50 km) with priority, wind direction and one-tap calls. The app matters for response: the warning reaches people even when they are not looking, so they can act early. Fires in Peru are often detected late; we turn a satellite pixel into a clear decision in seconds.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

Smart Forest Guardians turns NASA satellite data into wildfire information that anyone in Peru can understand and use. It has a website and an Android app.

• Near-real-time monitoring: every 10 minutes it downloads from the NASA FIRMS API the hotspots detected over Peru by VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) and MODIS (Terra and Aqua). It removes volcanoes, fixed heat sources (industries) and the ocean, and groups nearby hotspots into fires (1.5 km or less apart and 2 days or less apart). Each fire shows its strength (FRP in megawatts), its area, whether it is still active, wind, temperature and humidity (with their 24-hour history), air quality (Peru's official INCA index from MINAM), a spread forecast based on terrain, vegetation and wind, protected areas, and nearby resources: fire stations, health centers, water and roads.

• Harmonized burning calendar: we store the FIRMS archive since 2000 (2.4 million hotspots). Since VIIRS sees about 4 times more fires than MODIS, we calibrate it month by month to "MODIS-equivalent" and validate it by leaving one year out, so 2001 and 2024 can be compared fairly. Users choose any area (department, province, a drawn polygon or a radius) and dates; they see each month's activity, its anomaly versus a normal year and the burning season, and can download the results as CSV and PNG.

• My zone: using GPS (or a point chosen on the map), it analyzes a 50 or 100 km radius and gives a risk level with its reasons: distance, how long ago the fire was seen, its strength, nearby towns, the terrain (forest, cropland or urban area) and the wind. It recommends when to call the Firefighters, the Police or SERFOR (Peru's National Forest and Wildlife Service), and prepares a WhatsApp message with coordinates, distance, time, risk level and a map link, which the person reviews and approves before sending.

• AI assistant: a chat bubble answers, in simple Spanish, questions such as "Is there fire near me?", "Should I alert the authorities?", "How was 2024 in Ucayali?" or "What is the difference between MODIS and VIIRS?", using only real data from the user's area, from all of Peru and from the historical archive.

• Android app: it checks our alerts API every 15 minutes and sends a notification, even when nobody is looking at the map, when there is a fire within 20 km (citizens) or 50 km (firefighters), with its priority, the wind direction and a call button.

2. What benefits does it offer?

• For citizens: knowing in seconds whether there is fire nearby, how dangerous it is and whom to call, in simple words.

• For firefighters and police: fires sorted by priority, exact location, wind, access roads and nearby resources, plus alerts on their phones.

• For municipalities and SERFOR: seeing where and in which months burning repeats, comparing years fairly, and downloading data for reports and prevention plans.

• Everything in one place, free, on a phone or a computer, and with no invented data: it always reminds users that a hotspot seen by satellite must be confirmed on the ground.

3. What is the expected impact?

Reducing the time between the moment a satellite sees a fire and the moment someone acts: the alert reaches the phone and says whom to call. With the historical record, authorities can prepare before the burning season (July to October in much of the country) and prioritize the areas where fire keeps coming back. This helps protect forests, natural protected areas, crops and people's health from smoke. Example with real data: in 2024 Peru had about 10,900 fires, compared with about 8,700 in a normal year.

4. Tools, languages and software

• Web and server: Python (Flask, Waitress), SQLite for the historical archive, JavaScript with Leaflet, HTML and CSS.

• Mobile app: Kotlin with Android Studio, consuming our alerts API.

• NASA data: NASA FIRMS (near-real-time area API and standard processing, yearly country archive, MODIS and VIIRS), NASA GIBS, NASA Worldview and NASA EONET.

• Other open sources: Open-Meteo and MET Norway (weather), Copernicus CAMS (air quality), OpenStreetMap (towns, fire stations, health centers, roads), Esri Land Cover (vegetation) and Terrarium elevation data.

• Artificial intelligence: OpenRouter (Gemini 2.5 Flash model), called from the server without exposing keys.

• Cloud and development: Railway for hosting; ChatGPT and Claude supported us with programming and documentation.

5. In what way is it creative?

• It joins 25 years from two generations of satellites into a single comparable calendar, something that cannot be seen at a glance in the raw data.

• It goes from a "hot pixel" to a concrete decision: the risk level, whom to call and a ready-to-send message.

• An assistant that talks like a neighbor and answers with real NASA data, not invented answers.

• "In simple words" notes across the whole website, so anyone from a 10-year-old child to a public official can understand it.

• If a service fails, the website keeps working with backup sources.

6. What factors did the team consider?

• Accuracy: a hotspot is not always a fire; the website and the assistant always say so and never invent detections.

• Comparability: the switch from MODIS to VIIRS could make it look like there are more fires; that is why we harmonized and validated the data.

• Privacy and security: keys stay only on the server, the AI never receives the person's exact coordinates, and no message is sent without their approval.

• Accessibility: plain language, colorblind-safe colors, dark mode and a mobile-friendly design.

• Cost and continuity: free data sources, with automatic backups when one reaches its usage limit.

• Real users: citizens, municipal managers, firefighters, police and SERFOR, with configurable contact numbers.
